prompt: Write a note to a friend about garden tools that never seem to work. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the note only.
final_message:
Hey Sam,

I have to vent about my garden tools, because I've reached the point where I think they're plotting against me.

Start with the pruning shears. I paid actual money for them, the "professional grade" kind with the pretty orange handles. They worked for about three weeks. Now the blades stick halfway through every cut, so I end up gnawing at a rose cane like a beaver while the shears squeak in protest. I've oiled them, cleaned them and sharpened them. Nothing helps. I'm convinced they were assembled on a Friday afternoon.

Then there's the hose. Every spring I unroll it, and every spring it has sprung a leak somewhere along its sixty feet. I patch one spot with a repair coupling and it finds a new place to spray me. The nozzle is no better. It has six settings, and the only two that work are "dribble" and "sudden blast to the face."

The wheelbarrow tire has gone flat again. That's the third time this year. I'm fairly sure the tire isn't leaking so much as holding a grudge. I pump it up, load it with compost, make it halfway across the yard, and then it sighs and settles to the ground like a tired old dog.

And the trowel! The handle snapped clean off the first time I hit a stubborn root. A trowel's whole job is to dig, and mine couldn't take one tough carrot. Now I use a serving spoon from the kitchen, which works better than it has any right to, though I'd rather not explain that to anyone who asks.

I'll admit that part of this might be my own doing. I leave things out in the rain, I forget to drain the hose before winter, and I once used the shears to cut a piece of wire. But it still feels like the tools should be more forgiving. Gardening is supposed to be relaxing, and mine mostly involves muttering.

Anyway, I'm told you have a good set of tools that actually work. If you're willing to lend me a spade, or just tell me what brand to buy, I'll bring tea and some of the tomatoes that survived all this. Come by this weekend and see the carnage for yourself.

Talk soon,
[name]
